crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

children.name: Evidence Extraction Tables
children.blurb: Evidence extraction tables are structured summaries that pull key claims, study designs, populations, interventions, outcomes, and effect sizes from primary research into a comparable grid.

children.name: Weighing the Scientific Consensus
children.blurb: Weighing the scientific consensus means assessing how much agreement exists across published AI research on a given question, and how strong that agreement is.

children.name: Questioning Your Own Sources
children.blurb: Questioning your own sources means treating every paper, claim, and model output as provisional until its provenance, method, and conflicts have been checked.

children.name: Deep Research Agents and Landscape Scans
children.blurb: Deep research agents and landscape scans automate the early stages of literature review and evidence synthesis, from finding relevant work to mapping how papers, claims, models, tools, and books relate.

children.name: Translating Between Disciplines
children.blurb: Translating between disciplines means taking findings, methods, or terminology from one research field and restating them so they can be used in another.

sections.body: Literature review and evidence synthesis is the work of turning a scattered body of research into a clear picture of what is known, what is contested, and what is still missing. Artificial intelligence now does real extraction work here, pulling claims, sample sizes, effect directions, and study designs out of papers into structured tables. It also clusters findings by topic, flags contradictions between studies, and drafts plain language summaries of individual results. The site's own library holds 135 research papers and 11,075 extracted claims, which shows the kind of volume this work now handles. This is not a future promise, it is routine text processing applied to scientific prose.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: The solved parts are narrow but real. Extracting simple, well formatted claims from abstracts and results sections works reliably, and grouping papers by shared keywords or citation links is mature. What is not solved is the harder judgement work. AI can count how many papers report a positive result, but it cannot yet weigh a messy scientific consensus, judge whether a study was well designed, or notice when a field's shared assumptions are wrong. Honest limits include hallucinated citations, missed nuance in hedging language, and a tendency to treat every extracted claim as equally trustworthy. The tools are good at surfacing material, not at deciding what it means.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: A reader should start with Evidence Extraction Tables to see how raw claims become structured rows and columns, then move to Weighing the Scientific Consensus for the harder problem of deciding what the collected evidence actually supports. Questioning Your Own Sources turns the lens back on the reader's own reference list, showing how AI can help spot weak or circular citations. Deep Research Agents and Landscape Scans covers the broad sweep, where AI is used to map a whole field quickly rather than read a few papers closely. Translating Between Disciplines closes the loop by showing how the same extracted claims can be rephrased for researchers in another field, which is where synthesis becomes communication.
